Antidepressants are mostly used to treat
depression
in adults. They’re often prescribed with a talking therapy like
cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)
.
Antidepressants can also treat other
mental health conditions
and
long-term pain
.
How antidepressants work
Antidepressants are thought to work by increasing neurotransmitters like serotonin and noradrenaline. These are chemicals in the brain which can improve mood and emotion. But this process isn’t fully understood.
Increasing levels of neurotransmitters can also disrupt pain signals sent by nerves. This may explain why some antidepressants can help long-term pain.
Although antidepressants can treat depression symptoms, they don’t always address its causes. This is why they’re usually used along with therapy.
Types of antidepressants
There are different types of antidepressants, including:
selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)
serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs)
noradrenaline and specific serotonergic antidepressants (NASSAs)
tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs)
How to take antidepressants
Antidepressants are usually taken in tablet form. If you’re prescribed antidepressants, you’ll usually start on a low dose.
Antidepressants usually need to be taken for 7 to 14 days before the benefits are felt.
If you take antidepressants for 4 weeks and don’t feel any benefit, speak to your healthcare professional.
If you get some mild side effects early on, you should continue to take your antidepressants. These side effects usually wear off quickly. If you experience any severe side effects, you should let your specialist know.
A course of treatment usually lasts for 6 months. Some people with depression that keeps coming back may be advised to take them for longer.
Missed or extra doses
It’s important that you don’t miss any of your medication. This could make your treatment less effective.
If you do miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless it’s almost time to take your next dose. In this case, you should skip the missed dose. Don’t take a double dose to make up for the one you missed.
You should not take more than your prescribed dose unless you’re advised to by your doctor.
If you do take an extra dose by mistake, check with your pharmacist or medical professional. You can also phone 111 for advice.
Possible side effects
Antidepressants can cause side effects at first, but these usually improve with time.
For more information about your specific medication, read the patient information leaflet.
Common side effects
Common side effects of SSRIs and SNRIs can include:
feeling agitated, shaky or anxious
feeling and being sick
indigestion
stomach aches
diarrhoea
constipation
loss of appetite
dizziness
not sleeping well (insomnia)
, or feeling very sleepy
headaches
low sex drive
difficulties achieving orgasm during sex or masturbation
in men, difficulties getting or maintaining an erection
(erectile dysfunction)
These side effects should improve within a few weeks, although some may persist.
Common side effects of TCAs can include:
dry mouth
slight blurring of vision
constipation
problems passing urine (peeing)
drowsiness
dizziness
weight gain
excessive sweating
(especially at night)
heart rhythm problems, like noticeable
palpitations
or a
fast heartbeat (tachycardia)
Less common side effects
Serotonin syndrome
is a set of side effects linked to SSRIs and SNRIs. It isn’t common but it can be serious.
Elderly people can have low salt levels as a side effect of taking antidepressants. This is known as
hyponatraemia
. It may lead to a build-up of fluid inside the cells of the body which can be dangerous.
Warnings and precautions
Antidepressants can interact with:
alcohol – your symptoms may get worse, and with some types of antidepressant can make you drowsy and dizzy
illegal drugs – your symptoms may get worse, and they can cause unpredictable and unpleasant side effects
St John’s Wort – taking it with other medications can cause serious health problems
other antidepressants – you should never take 2 different types of antidepressants together, unless advised to by a healthcare professional
Other medicines and antidepressants
Antidepressants can react unpredictably with other medications, including over-the-counter medications like
ibuprofen
. Always read the patient information leaflet that comes with your medication. This will let you know if there are any medications you should avoid.
If you’re unsure, your pharmacist or GP should be able to help.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding
Antidepressants are not usually recommended if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding. Sometimes exceptions will be made.
You should discuss using antidepressants with your doctor or healthcare professional.
Driving and using machinery
Some antidepressants can cause dizziness, drowsiness and blurred vision. These symptoms usually happen when you first start taking antidepressants.
If you do experience these problems, you should avoid driving, using tools or operating machinery.
Stopping antidepressants
You should not suddenly stop taking antidepressants, even if you feel better. If your GP or specialist decides to stop your antidepressants, they’ll reduce the dose slowly over a few weeks.
Stopping antidepressants suddenly can lead to withdrawal symptoms like:
stomach upsets
flu-like symptoms
anxiety
dizziness
sensations in the body that feel like electric shocks
seizures (fits)
Coming off antidepressants too soon can also cause your condition to return. It may mean the medication hasn’t had a chance to take effect.
Alternatives to antidepressants
There are alternatives to antidepressants. This includes
talking therapies
like:
cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)
interpersonal therapy (IPT)
counselling
self-help groups
These may be used to manage depression and other mental health conditions.
Other alternatives to antidepressants include:
exercise
lithium
electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
